My quest to become a real estate agent

It's shockingly easy to get a real estate license. That should terrify America's homebuyers.

By James Rodriguez

On a recent autumn morning, I filed into a cramped classroom on the seventh floor of a government building near Wall Street, poised to take my first meaningful test in nearly a decade. If I passed, I would gain entry to a not-so-exclusive, though potentially lucrative, century-old club. I was there to get my real estate license.

Alongside a few dozen aspiring agents, I spent the next hour and 15 minutes grasping for far-flung bits of knowledge — the definition of a joist, the equation for the area of a triangle, the parts of a home where you're most likely to find asbestos (pipe insulation, if you're wondering). A mere 75 multiple-choice questions stood between me and "essentially unlimited income potential," as one of my online instructors had put it. Maybe some in the room would go on to fulfill that promise, but statistically speaking, most of us were destined to end up fodder for the vast machine that keeps the industry stocked with inexperienced, low-earning real estate agents.

The machine is remarkably efficient. There are at least 1.4 million real estate licensees in the US, more than the number of lawyers, plumbers, or active-duty military personnel. To get one of these licenses, most states require just a few weeks of self-paced online coursework and a passing grade on a multiple-choice test. In New York, where I live, becoming a nail technician requires 250 hours of classes and both written and practical examinations. A certification as a court stenographer demands 1,300 hours of private instruction and proof that you can type out 225 words per minute. To advise someone on one of life's biggest financial transactions, I had to sit through 77 hours of online instructional videos and score above 70% on a brief exam. It didn't matter if I failed on my first attempt — or second, third, or fourth. In New York, where the pass rate hovers around 50%, you can take the exam as many times as necessary, with no required waiting period in between. As my fellow test takers marched into the room, one of them greeted the proctors warmly: "I see you guys more than I see my family at this point!"

Thousands of career-switchers, stay-at-home moms, and budding moguls will trace a similar path this year. A good chunk of them will close only a deal or two in their first year on the job, if any at all. This is a feature, not a bug. The entire industry, from giants like the National Association of Realtors and Zillow down to your friendly local brokerage, relies on this numbers game. The sheer volume of agents is simply good business.

Real estate agents are trusted less than bankers, building contractors, and, to my surprise, journalists: Just 17% of Americans rate their honesty and ethical standards as "high" or "very high," Gallup polling shows. After years of listening to industry boosters and consumer advocates argue, I wanted a definitive answer to whether this low licensing bar puts homebuyers and sellers in harm's way. To resolve the debate, I figured I'd go through the process myself. What I saw wasn't pretty.

The first thing I learned about real-estate school is that there are many, many real-estate schools. In New York, dozens of state-approved educators are vying for your business — places like the American Real Estate Institute, American Real Estate School, New York Real Estate Institute, and Realty Institute, all of which appear to be separate operations. I went with a company called RealEstateU, which, for $277, offered a 77-hour online course, a few practice exams for the state test, and a "How to Start a Successful Career in Real Estate" class.

I hoped the classes might illuminate the tricks of the trade and reveal the indispensable knowledge only a real-estate agent can provide. I had, and still have, no plans to use my license on behalf of a client. But maybe all those hours would come in handy if I ever bought a place of my own. Alas, this was not the case.

Instead, the classes offer a crash course in real estate law, middle-school-level math, housing finance, and the various environmental scourges — asbestos, mold, polychlorinated biphenyls — that could threaten real estate values. Over 19 chapters ranging from land-use regulations to taxes, I trudged through the minutiae underpinning every home sale. I was struck by what the modules didn't cover: negotiation skills, a step-by-step guide to a transaction, and where things most often go wrong. Rather than showing me how to secure the best deal for a client, the classes harped on what not to do — the violations that could land you and your broker in hot water. The instructional videos often wrapped up before the on-page timer let me move on, leaving me to fidget with my phone or hop to another tab while the clock ran out. And nearly 20 hours were allotted for quizzes that took me a fraction of that time. I may have had a slight head start as a reporter covering real estate. But judging by online discussions about the course, I wasn't alone.

Years from now, I may not recall the difference between an easement appurtenant and an easement in gross. I will, however, remember the head-scratching moments that yanked me from my stupor: when one instructor, for instance, referred to "the real estate crash a couple of years ago," helping me date these videos to the early 2010s. Or the time when we wrapped a hefty module on fair housing — an area in which the real estate industry has a sordid track record — and the very next chapter began with a segment on how to calculate our commissions.

As with so many professions, the licensing process covers a lot of facts and figures that don't reflect the real life of a professional. "The stuff you learn to get your license, you don't really use in your daily practice," says Lissa Lebel, a former film executive who now works as an agent in California. After passing her exam, she joined a large brokerage and felt like she was "literally pushed out a window." It was scary, she says — not only for her, but for potential clients. "In the beginning, people didn't want to work with me," Lebel tells me. She understood why. Most agents get their training through their brokerage rather than the state-mandated classes, but those brokerages don't always hold up their end of the bargain. "Some brokers are like, 'Here's your license and you're good to go,'" says James Dwiggins, president of the real estate franchise NextHome. "And then the agent's trying to figure it out."

The stuff you'd really want to learn, like how to talk to a buyer or seller, or how to accurately price a home, appears nowhere in the state courses. "You're practicing for a multiple-choice test," says Bret Weinstein, a Denver broker and outspoken critic of the agent glut. "You are not practicing to help someone."

I should note that RealEstateU, like all state-approved educators, follows a specific curriculum handed down by New York regulators. Derek Abbott, RealEstateU's head of education and compliance, tells me in an email that understanding these foundational concepts "is essential to representing clients responsibly and protecting consumers," though distinct from "the practical experience necessary to become an effective real estate professional."

With such plentiful competition, it's no wonder that many agents fail to earn a livable wage, let alone the kinds of commission checks that could land them on "Selling Sunset," "Million Dollar Listing," or other reality shows that tout the glitzy side of the trade. The typical Realtor with two years of experience or less earned $8,000 last year before factoring in expenses, the NAR reported. Roughly 30% of all Realtors earned less than $25,000; among new Realtors, more than 75% fell into this category. Many agents work part-time, squeezing in showings between shuttling kids to soccer practice or putting food on the table via another job.

You're practicing for a multiple-choice test. You are not practicing to help someone.Bret Weinstein, Denver broker

I started my classes in April, chipping away an hour or so at a time while also keeping up with my day job. In September, I decided to pick up the pace, ramping the videos to 2x speed and churning through the quizzes. By the end of the month, I had cruised through the course's exam (a prerequisite for the state test) and passed several practice tests. It was time for the real thing.

Some questions stumped me: I couldn't recall the year that disability was added as a protected class under the Fair Housing Act (1988), whether a New York agent has to retake the state exam if they've let their license lapse within the past year (they don't), or which act curtailed the use of chlorofluorocarbons (the Clean Air Act). When I tallied up the questions I felt even mildly unsure about, though, I felt confident I had cleared the 54-question threshold for a passing grade. I handed in my test and walked out of the building.

Real estate's shot callers are all too aware of this system's drawbacks. In 2015, the NAR published the D.A.N.G.E.R. Report, or Definitive Analysis of Negative Game Changers Emerging in Real Estate, an exhaustive rundown of the threats keeping real estate execs up at night. Stefan Swanepoel, the founder of the real estate consultancy T3 Sixty and the author of the report, concluded that the top danger facing real estate agents wasn't tech disruption, pesky bureaucrats, or a collapse of the housing-finance system. It was other agents.

"The real estate industry is saddled with a large number of part-time, untrained, unethical, and/or incompetent agents," the report reads.

The report goes on to lambast the low barriers to entry and moneymaking promises that lure hordes of mediocre agents to the industry each year. Swanepoel tells me that the ease of obtaining a license remains a problem for unsuspecting homebuyers. In classic Western movies, he says, the bad guys wear black and the heroes don white. "In real estate, you can't tell the difference!" The system seems calibrated to signal to consumers that they're in capable hands — "Don't worry, I've got a license for this!" — without tipping into territory that would shrink the number of agents.

Real estate licenses are a fairly recent invention. In the early 20th century, the first incarnation of the National Association of Realtors began urging states to enact licensing requirements to distinguish conniving amateurs from trustworthy pros. Every state now requires a license, but the exact criteria for obtaining one vary. Some states demand more than 100 hours of education — others, as little as 40. Swanepoel estimates that the average education requirement across all states has inched up in the past decade, from 70 hours to roughly 80 hours, though he regards this as little more than a rounding error.

"The industry has given education a thumbs down," Swanepoel says. "It just doesn't care."

Couldn't the NAR, which spent about $54 million last year on lobbying, push states to add rigor? The organization tells me in an emailed statement that it has "long been committed to raising the bar for professionalism in the industry" through its code of ethics as well as ongoing training and education in areas such as fair housing. There's another powerful reason, though, that the NAR and other power players might feel less than motivated to push for change: The numbers work in their favor.

The industry has given education a thumbs down. It just doesn't care.Stefan Swanepoel, founder of the real estate consultancy T3 Sixty

Though real estate agents can technically ply their trade without becoming a "Realtor" — the term is trademarked by the NAR — most working agents belong to the group. It's not hard to join: Once you've got a license, becoming a Realtor requires little more than taking a 2.5-hour ethics course and paying roughly $200 a year in dues. The NAR boasts more than 1.4 million members, close to an all-time high; dues accounted for about 84% of the nonprofit's $361 million in revenue in 2024. The flood of agents also feeds real-estate portals like Zillow and Realtor.com, which sell them leads on potential clients, as well as a cottage industry of sales coaches and software services.

"There's no incentive for this to change," says Mike DelPrete, a real estate tech strategist and scholar-in-residence at the University of Colorado Boulder. "You can't point to any one body, or company, or anyone that's actually incentivized for the barriers to entry to change."

Five days after my exam, I logged into my online portal to check my results. On a sparse state government website, under "Exam Result," there was no score or letter grade, just one word: "Pass."

Once you pass, there's one more hoop you have to jump through: finding a broker to "sponsor" you. If you've ever signed an agreement to have an agent list your home or represent you on the hunt, you probably entered into a contract with their broker, even if you didn't realize it. In New York, as in most states, the broker designation requires more education, another test, and experience actually closing deals. The agent operates more or less independently, piecing together the transaction and negotiating on your behalf, while the broker is more of a legal backstop, theoretically preventing things from going off the rails and offering backend support.

Brokerages, especially large, nationwide firms like Keller Williams, Century 21, and Coldwell Banker, are arguably the largest beneficiaries of the agent churn. The nationwide brands license their names for a fee to thousands of local franchise offices, who, in turn, take a percentage of their agent's commissions. The local brokers often demand the biggest cuts from their least experienced salespeople — sometimes as much as half. Since the vast majority of agents are independent contractors, they require little overhead. Brokerages may also charge their agents monthly "desk fees," "technology fees," or "coaching fees" to keep revenue flowing from slow sellers and offset other costs, such as office space or admin staff. A marginal agent may not reach their dream of a six-figure income, but if they close even a couple of deals for their cousin or neighbor, a brokerage will be happy to keep them around.

It's harder to say whether those clients — "friends, family, and fools," as one broker put it to me — end up with a good deal. Agents generally command 2% to 3% of the home's sale price, regardless of experience level or quality of service. And while the low barrier to entry may not set up salespeople for success, "the potential for consumer harm is there, as well," says Summer Goralik, a real estate compliance consultant in California. A buyer or seller may never realize if they overpaid for a home, missed out on a better property, or if their agent's fumbling meant the whole thing simply dragged on too long. "Many screw-ups are not visible at all," says Stephen Brobeck, a senior fellow at the Consumer Policy Center. "The consumer never knows."

A Zillow spokesperson disputed the suggestion that it relies on sheer agent volume, saying that "who we work with matters" and noting that its main program for agents, Zillow Preferred, is invite-only. Jason Abrams, chief industry and strategy officer at Keller Williams, says the company spends a lot of money on offices, admin, and agent training, pushing back on the idea that brokerages like his benefit from an unfettered flow of new agents. Abrams also points to NAR data that shows most buyers and sellers say they'd work with their real estate agent again.

"When the consumer of that industry is no longer satisfied with the product, you see wholesale change," Abrams tells me. "Today, I don't see that."

Many brokerages appear to be continually fishing for new agents on places like Craigslist, Facebook, or Indeed. Some promise hands-on mentorship, fewer monthly fees, or friendlier commission splits. RealEstateU included on its website a handful of suggested brokerages. I emailed one of them, Manhattan-based DiGiulio, and explained my project. Justin DiGiulio, the owner and principal broker, responded within an hour: "Sounds like a great story!" When we met in his eighth-floor office a couple of weeks later, he reflected on the first brokerage he joined, more than 15 years ago. "My first interview, the guy talked to me for an hour and then hired me," DiGiulio told me. "And I was, like, ecstatic. Let's go out for drinks, that type of thing. I was so happy. Now I realize pretty much any brokerage will hire anybody."

Once DiGiulio agreed to be my sponsoring broker, the state approved my online license application within hours. In my capacity as a newly minted real estate agent, I still wasn't sure what I was doing. DiGiulio was both unsurprised and unbothered by this. He runs his own training course for new agents, where he coaches them on everything from how to pitch condo developers to the kinds of shoes they should wear. "They're teaching you the laws," he said of the licensing classes. "They don't teach you how to do the business. So when you get started as an agent, then you have to learn how to make money."

My two weeks' worth of classes were good for a few things: a peek behind the curtain of a $150 billion industry, a glimpse of the business incentives that put both agents and consumers at a disadvantage, and, crucially, the ability to call myself a licensed salesperson. Mostly, though, they left me with the gnawing feeling that I would struggle to close a deal on my own behalf, let alone for an anxious hypothetical client. More than ever, I wanted someone in my corner who knew the process inside and out, who could unlock hidden doors in the market, harangue on my behalf, and help me steer clear of traps. I wanted, in other words, a real estate agent.

The local brokers often demand the biggest cuts from their least experienced salespeople — sometimes as much as half. Since the vast majority of agents are independent contractors, they require little overhead. Brokerages may also charge their agents monthly "desk fees," "technology fees," or "coaching fees" to keep revenue flowing from slow sellers and offset other costs, such as office space or admin staff. A marginal agent may not reach their dream of a six-figure income, but if they close even a couple of deals for their cousin or neighbor, a brokerage will be happy to keep them around.It's harder to say whether those clients — "friends, family, and fools," as one broker put it to me — end up with a good deal. Agents generally command 2% to 3% of the home's sale price, regardless of experience level or quality of service. And while the low barrier to entry may not set up salespeople for success, "the potential for consumer harm is there, as well," says Summer Goralik, a real estate compliance consultant in California. A buyer or seller may never realize if they overpaid for a home, missed out on a better property, or if their agent's fumbling meant the whole thing simply dragged on too long. "Many screw-ups are not visible at all," says Stephen Brobeck, a senior fellow at the Consumer Policy Center. "The consumer never knows."A Zillow spokesperson disputed the suggestion that it relies on sheer agent volume, saying that "who we work with matters" and noting that its main program for agents, Zillow Preferred, is invite-only. Jason Abrams, chief industry and strategy officer at Keller Williams, says the company spends a lot of money on offices, admin, and agent training, pushing back on the idea that brokerages like his benefit from an unfettered flow of new agents. Abrams also points to NAR data that shows most buyers and sellers say they'd work with their real estate agent again."When the consumer of that industry is no longer satisfied with the product, you see wholesale change," Abrams tells me. "Today, I don't see that."Many brokerages appear to be continually fishing for new agents on places like Craigslist, Facebook, or Indeed. Some promise hands-on mentorship, fewer monthly fees, or friendlier commission splits. RealEstateU included on its website a handful of suggested brokerages. I emailed one of them, Manhattan-based DiGiulio, and explained my project. Justin DiGiulio, the owner and principal broker, responded within an hour: "Sounds like a great story!" When we met in his eighth-floor office a couple of weeks later, he reflected on the first brokerage he joined, more than 15 years ago. "My first interview, the guy talked to me for an hour and then hired me," DiGiulio told me. "And I was, like, ecstatic. Let's go out for drinks, that type of thing. I was so happy. Now I realize pretty much any brokerage will hire anybody." Justin DiGiulio (left), the author's sponsoring broker, says the classes don't teach you "how to do the business." Laila AnnMarie Stevens for BI Once DiGiulio agreed to be my sponsoring broker, the state approved my online license application within hours. In my capacity as a newly minted real estate agent, I still wasn't sure what I was doing. DiGiulio was both unsurprised and unbothered by this. He runs his own training course for new agents, where he coaches them on everything from how to pitch condo developers to the kinds of shoes they should wear. "They're teaching you the laws," he said of the licensing classes. "They don't teach you how to do the business. So when you get started as an agent, then you have to learn how to make money."My two weeks' worth of classes were good for a few things: a peek behind the curtain of a $150 billion industry, a glimpse of the business incentives that put both agents and consumers at a disadvantage, and, crucially, the ability to call myself a licensed salesperson. Mostly, though, they left me with the gnawing feeling that I would struggle to close a deal on my own behalf, let alone for an anxious hypothetical client. More than ever, I wanted someone in my corner who knew the process inside and out, who could unlock hidden doors in the market, harangue on my behalf, and help me steer clear of traps. blocks.html_en: The machine is remarkably efficient. There are at least 1.4 million real estate licensees in the US, more than the number of lawyers, plumbers, or active-duty military personnel. To get one of these licenses, most states require just a few weeks of self-paced online coursework and a passing grade on a multiple-choice test. In New York, where I live, becoming a nail technician requires 250 hours of classes and both written and practical examinations. A certification as a court stenographer demands 1,300 hours of private instruction and proof that you can type out 225 words per minute. To advise someone on one of life's biggest financial transactions, I had to sit through 77 hours of online instructional videos and score above 70% on a brief exam. It didn't matter if I failed on my first attempt — or second, third, or fourth. In New York, where the pass rate hovers around 50%, you can take the exam as many times as necessary, with no required waiting period in between. As my fellow test takers marched into the room, one of them greeted the proctors warmly: "I see you guys more than I see my family at this point!"

It's shockingly easy to get a real estate license. That should terrify America's homebuyers.

By James Rodriguez You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

On a recent autumn morning, I filed into a cramped classroom on the seventh floor of a government building near Wall Street, poised to take my first meaningful test in nearly a decade. If I passed, I would gain entry to a not-so-exclusive, though potentially lucrative, century-old club. I was there to get my real estate license.

Alongside a few dozen aspiring agents, I spent the next hour and 15 minutes grasping for far-flung bits of knowledge — the definition of a joist, the equation for the area of a triangle, the parts of a home where you're most likely to find asbestos (pipe insulation, if you're wondering). A mere 75 multiple-choice questions stood between me and "essentially unlimited income potential," as one of my online instructors had put it. Maybe some in the room would go on to fulfill that promise, but statistically speaking, most of us were destined to end up fodder for the vast machine that keeps the industry stocked with inexperienced, low-earning real estate agents.

The machine is remarkably efficient. There are at least 1.4 million real estate licensees in the US, more than the number of lawyers, plumbers, or active-duty military personnel. To get one of these licenses, most states require just a few weeks of self-paced online coursework and a passing grade on a multiple-choice test. In New York, where I live, becoming a nail technician requires 250 hours of classes and both written and practical examinations. A certification as a court stenographer demands 1,300 hours of private instruction and proof that you can type out 225 words per minute. To advise someone on one of life's biggest financial transactions, I had to sit through 77 hours of online instructional videos and score above 70% on a brief exam. It didn't matter if I failed on my first attempt — or second, third, or fourth. In New York, where the pass rate hovers around 50%, you can take the exam as many times as necessary, with no required waiting period in between. As my fellow test takers marched into the room, one of them greeted the proctors warmly: "I see you guys more than I see my family at this point!"

Thousands of career-switchers, stay-at-home moms, and budding moguls will trace a similar path this year. A good chunk of them will close only a deal or two in their first year on the job, if any at all. This is a feature, not a bug. The entire industry, from giants like the National Association of Realtors and Zillow down to your friendly local brokerage, relies on this numbers game. The sheer volume of agents is simply good business.

Real estate agents are trusted less than bankers, building contractors, and, to my surprise, journalists: Just 17% of Americans rate their honesty and ethical standards as "high" or "very high," Gallup polling shows. After years of listening to industry boosters and consumer advocates argue, I wanted a definitive answer to whether this low licensing bar puts homebuyers and sellers in harm's way. To resolve the debate, I figured I'd go through the process myself. What I saw wasn't pretty.

The first thing I learned about real-estate school is that there are many, many real-estate schools. In New York, dozens of state-approved educators are vying for your business — places like the American Real Estate Institute, American Real Estate School, New York Real Estate Institute, and Realty Institute, all of which appear to be separate operations. I went with a company called RealEstateU, which, for $277, offered a 77-hour online course, a few practice exams for the state test, and a "How to Start a Successful Career in Real Estate" class.

I hoped the classes might illuminate the tricks of the trade and reveal the indispensable knowledge only a real-estate agent can provide. I had, and still have, no plans to use my license on behalf of a client. But maybe all those hours would come in handy if I ever bought a place of my own. Alas, this was not the case.

Instead, the classes offer a crash course in real estate law, middle-school-level math, housing finance, and the various environmental scourges — asbestos, mold, polychlorinated biphenyls — that could threaten real estate values. Over 19 chapters ranging from land-use regulations to taxes, I trudged through the minutiae underpinning every home sale. I was struck by what the modules didn't cover: negotiation skills, a step-by-step guide to a transaction, and where things most often go wrong. Rather than showing me how to secure the best deal for a client, the classes harped on what not to do — the violations that could land you and your broker in hot water. The instructional videos often wrapped up before the on-page timer let me move on, leaving me to fidget with my phone or hop to another tab while the clock ran out. And nearly 20 hours were allotted for quizzes that took me a fraction of that time. I may have had a slight head start as a reporter covering real estate. But judging by online discussions about the course, I wasn't alone.

Years from now, I may not recall the difference between an easement appurtenant and an easement in gross. Or the time when we wrapped a hefty module on fair housing — an area in which the real estate industry has a sordid track record — and the very next chapter began with a segment on how to calculate our commissions.

As with so many professions, the licensing process covers a lot of facts and figures that don't reflect the real life of a professional. When I tallied up the questions I felt even mildly unsure about, though, I felt confident I had cleared the 54-question threshold for a passing grade. I handed in my test and walked out of the building.

It was other agents.

"The real estate industry is saddled with a large number of part-time, untrained, unethical, and/or incompetent agents," the report reads.

The report goes on to lambast the low barriers to entry and moneymaking promises that lure hordes of mediocre agents to the industry each year. Swanepoel tells me that the ease of obtaining a license remains a problem for unsuspecting homebuyers. In classic Western movies, he says, the bad guys wear black and the heroes don white. The system seems calibrated to signal to consumers that they're in capable hands — "Don't worry, I've got a license for this!" — without tipping into territory that would shrink the number of agents.

"They're teaching you the laws," he said of the licensing classes. "They don't teach you how to do the business. So when you get started as an agent, then you have to learn how to make money."

My two weeks' worth of classes were good for a few things: a peek behind the curtain of a $150 billion industry, a glimpse of the business incentives that put both agents and consumers at a disadvantage, and, crucially, the ability to call myself a licensed salesperson. Mostly, though, they left me with the gnawing feeling that I would struggle to close a deal on my own behalf, let alone for an anxious hypothetical client. More than ever, I wanted someone in my corner who knew the process inside and out, who could unlock hidden doors in the market, harangue on my behalf, and help me steer clear of traps. I wanted, in other words, a real estate agent.
